segs.text: Can vibration cut stone? In a factory, today, yes. Can sound cut or lift the stones of a pyramid? That is a different claim. This episode keeps the two apart: what engineers have published, what experiments with ancient tools found, what people claim, and what would settle it.

First, the real method. It is called ultrasonic machining. A metal tool vibrates along its length, typically twenty to forty thousand times a second, at or above the edge of human hearing, by a tiny fraction of a millimetre. Between the tool and the work flows a slurry: water full of hard grit, such as silicon carbide or boron carbide. Each vibration drives grit grains into the surface. In a hard, brittle material, each hit chips off a speck. Millions of specks later, there is a hole in the shape of the tool.

Notice who does most of the cutting. Not the tool. The loose grit. The tool supplies and shapes the impacts, and it is usually ordinary steel, softer than the glass or ceramic it cuts. Vibration is a way to keep slamming fresh grit into the surface, again and again.

None of this is anyone's personal discovery. A 1927 paper by Robert Wood and Alfred Loomis is credited with first discussing ultrasonic machining. A British patent application was filed in 1945 by Industrial Research Corporation, and histories link it to Lewis Balamuth. An American patent to Balamuth is listed as issued in 1952. Machines appeared in the early to mid nineteen fifties. A 1998 review by Thoe, Aspinwall and Wise, in the International Journal of Machine Tools and Manufacture, surveys decades of work.

It has limits. It works best on hard, brittle materials: glass, ceramics, gemstones, stone. Ductile metals tend to deform instead of chipping, so it is usually less efficient on them. It is slow. It makes holes and cavities, usually in small parts, and deep holes are hard, because fresh slurry struggles to reach the bottom. And it needs a power supply and a transducer, piezoelectric or magnetostrictive, to turn electricity into vibration. Conventional ultrasonic machining is used for holes and cavities. It is not documented as a way to quarry large blocks.

Now the ancient side. Some Egyptian granite sarcophagi carry saw cuts, recorded by Flinders Petrie in the eighteen eighties and by others since. Granite is hard, and the craftsmen had copper tools. How? In 1999 the experimental archaeologist Denys Stocks tested it at the Aswan quarries, and reported in Antiquity in 2001. His copper blade was one point eight metres long, with quartz sand under it, and two people pulling it back and forth.

It cut. Slowly: about twelve cubic centimetres of granite an hour, dry or wet, and he suggested that experience could double that. The sand did the cutting; the soft copper just carried it, and the copper wore away too. It shows what can work. It does not prove what the Egyptians did.

Look at the family resemblance. Egyptian sand sawing and ultrasonic machining both drive hard grit into hard stone with a softer tool. The difference is the motion. By hand, it is a stroke or two a second, our own estimate. Ultrasonic machining is twenty thousand or more. That is roughly ten thousand times the vibration rate. Not a comparison of cutting speed. They share one broad principle: loose abrasive between a softer tool and the stone.

Now the claim. Some authors argue the Egyptians used ultrasonic drilling. The best known version is the engineer Christopher Dunn, in a 1984 magazine article. He compared a spiral cut that Petrie measured in a granite core with the feed rate of a modern diamond drill, and concluded the ancient rate was about five hundred times greater. Experimental archaeologists have tested copper tubes with sand, and cut granite. In the literature we read, we found no ancient transducer, no power source, and no text describing one. Claimed. Not established.

The other claim is bigger: that sound lifted the blocks. A modern story, usually set in Tibet, describes drums and trumpets floating stones. Episode two met the same idea at Coral Castle. We found no film, measurement or physical trace we could check. What does real acoustic levitation do? In labs, sound waves hold small, light things in the air. One published far field demonstration held a thirty millimetre foam ball weighing six tenths of a gram. A close range method has carried several kilograms, but only tens to hundreds of micrometres above a vibrating surface.

Here is our own rough arithmetic. An average Great Pyramid block is about two and a third tonnes, an estimate. Hold one up with sound under one flat square metre. Even with perfect reflection, you would need roughly one hundred eighty six decibels. The limit for air itself is roughly one hundred ninety one to one hundred ninety four, depending on convention, where the low pressure half of the wave would reach a vacuum. And the block weighs almost four million times that foam ball. That does not prove it impossible. It shows the size of the gap.

What would a strong test look like? For cutting: independent labs comparing tool marks on ancient stone with marks from known methods. For lifting: a recorded demonstration with a stone of known weight and measured sound levels, repeated by a second team. And a bench test: copper, grit and soft stone, the same minutes with vibration on and off, then measure the groove. Our rough plan uses an ultrasonic cleaner, which is not a real machining rig, so it would be a first look. We have not run it: no result.

So here is the ledger. Documented: ultrasonic machining cuts hard, brittle materials. Some Egyptian granite objects carry saw cuts. Copper and sand cut granite, slowly, in Stocks's tests. Disputed: how the drill holes were made, and Dunn's feed rate comparison. Claimed: that ancient builders used ultrasonic tools. Not established: that sound cut or lifted pyramid stones. Unknown here: whether vibration speeds up copper and sand cutting, because our test has not been run.

So, can vibration cut stone? Yes: conventional ultrasonic machining does, with loose grit, a transducer, and electricity. Did anyone do it in the pyramid age? Not established. Did sound lift pyramid blocks? Not established, and the arithmetic is steep. Not ruled out, either: new evidence could settle it. If you can run a test, someone watching this might be the one who shows us.
